A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-model sensitivity study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and formatting.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C.3 report original DPO experiments with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and zephyr-7b-alpha on synthetic animal preferences, including results across three random seeds.

after.justification: The original experiments remain. Appendices C.4–C.5 additionally report a non-dominant-preference control, reward-model measurements on conversation data, and a constructed preference-reversal example.

M1.justification: The preference-model formulations and DPO training procedure are retained. The additions concern evaluation and case-study construction; they introduce no new proposed model architecture, objective, or inference algorithm.

E1.justification: v1's empirical coverage consists of synthetic dog/cat/bird preferences. Appendix C.5 adds Anthropic/hh-rlhf conversation data and a harmful-response case study, substantially extending coverage to real conversational preferences.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates a proposed algorithm against competing baselines. The newly examined Nemotron and DeBERTa reward models are subjects of sensitivity analysis rather than additions to a baseline comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 adds a Llama control with pD12 = 0.5 alongside the retained 0.99 setting. Appendix C.5 introduces scoring 8,552 test examples with two pretrained reward models, binning score-derived probabilities, and selecting and rewriting responses using probability thresholds. The original DPO and 200-query evaluation settings remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether weaker dominance mitigates sensitivity, how frequently existing reward models express dominant preferences, and whether response rewrites can reverse a safety-relevant preference. These appear in Figure C5 and Tables C2–C3; v1's existing Zephyr replication is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three random-seed runs with shaded one-standard-deviation bands for the synthetic experiments. Figure C5 follows this existing practice; no changed run counts or new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and C4 retain their original pL13 and pL23 curves and add pL12 results. New results include Figure C5, Table C2's 1,795 Nemotron and 167 DeBERTa probabilities in [0.99, 1.00), and Table C3's constructed preference reversal from 0.9526 to 0.4378 after rewriting a response. These are additional findings, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The core assumptions, sensitivity theorems, and Appendix B proofs are retained. Appendix C.5.1 adds Gaussian-score reasoning leading to logit-normal preference probabilities and a variance-dependent transition between unimodal and bimodal densities.

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contributions retain their meaning. The conclusion newly extends the implications to other systems using preference models, explicitly including Chatbot Arena, modestly broadening the claimed applicability.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly states that non-transitive human preferences outside the Plackett-Luce framework are not covered. It also adds a reward-score-variance explanation for dominant probabilities. The existing robustness–dominance tradeoff and caveats about transferring theory to LLMs remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.5 identifies and links the reward-model checkpoints and documents the conversation-data split, sample count, score conversion, and response-construction steps. Existing GPU specifications, optimizer, DPO hyperparameters, and synthetic-data templates are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds reward-hacking references in Section 5, plus references supporting Chatbot Arena applicability, non-transitive preferences, the conversation dataset, and reward-model checkpoints. The broader related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include adding 'Preference Models' to the title, local explanatory and grammatical edits, acknowledgements and ethics/reproducibility statements, and new Appendix C subsections.

P2.justification: The document adopts ICLR formatting with different typography, text width, author placement, headers, and figure placement. It adds Figure C5 and Tables C2–C3; Figures 3 and C4 gain a third series and triangle/square markers with captions distinguishing dataset-specified and unspecified preferences.

improvement.justification: The non-dominant control and pretrained reward-model analyses strengthen v1's empirical support, which was limited to synthetic animal preferences. The explicit non-transitivity limitation also clarifies applicability. The real-world failure demonstration remains one constructed example, so the gains in practical validation are useful but limited.
